$comment: Advisories that are acknowledged but deliberately not fixed, with a reason and an expiry.
An entry only suppresses the exact advisory id listed. Anything else high/critical still fails CI.
An expired entry FAILS the build on purpose — it forces a re-review rather than rotting silently.
Keep this list as short as you can. Prefer upgrading over allowlisting.

allow.reason: RSC Mode CSRF bypass. Only exploitable via the unstable React Server Components APIs (per the advisory: 'This only affects your application if you are using the unstable RSC APIs'). This app is a client-only Vite SPA using createBrowserRouter + RouterProvider (frontend/src/app/routes.tsx, frontend/src/app/App.tsx) and imports no RSC API, so the vulnerable code path is unreachable.
allow.noFixAvailable: There is no patched 7.x release. The fix landed only in react-router 8.3.0, which requires React >=19.2.7; this app is on React 18.3.1, so adopting it means a full React 19 migration. npm's suggested 'fix' is a downgrade to react-router-dom@7.11.0, which would drop seven minor releases of genuine fixes to mitigate a vulnerability that does not apply.
allow.reviewAction: Re-evaluate when the frontend moves to React 19 — at that point upgrade to react-router 8.3.0+ and delete this entry.

allow.reason: Stack exhaustion (uncontrolled recursion) that only triggers when deepmerge-ts merges an attacker-controlled, deeply-recursive object graph. deepmerge-ts is a build/dev-time transitive of @prisma/config (the Prisma CLI / migration tooling), not part of the running Express app, and is never invoked on runtime request data. The vulnerable code path is therefore unreachable in production — it can at most affect a developer's own machine during prisma generate / migrate.
allow.noFixAvailable: No published @prisma/config release yet depends on a patched deepmerge-ts, so there is no non-breaking upgrade. `npm audit fix --force` would downgrade Prisma's tooling and risk breaking migrations/generation.
allow.reviewAction: Remove when @prisma/config ships a build that pulls a patched deepmerge-ts (run `npm audit` to confirm the advisory is gone), then delete this entry.

allow.reason: MySQL2 auth-plugin downgrade to mysql_clear_password can leak plaintext DB credentials to a malicious or spoofed MySQL server. mysql2 is only present because the Prisma CLI (prisma@7.9.1) bundles connectors for every datasource. This app is PostgreSQL-only: the Prisma datasource is `postgresql` and the running Express server connects exclusively through the pg driver adapter (@prisma/adapter-pg). mysql2 is never imported or used to open a MySQL connection, so the vulnerable auth-negotiation path is unreachable at both build time and runtime.
allow.noFixAvailable: The advisory is fixed in mysql2 >=3.22.0, but prisma@7.9.1 pins mysql2@3.15.3 transitively and there is no patched Prisma 7.x release yet. npm's suggested 'fix' is a downgrade to prisma@6.19.3 (a major-version downgrade) which would break the driver-adapter setup and migrations. A manual `overrides: { mysql2: '^3.22.0' }` is possible but touches the lockfile for a package we never load.
allow.reviewAction: Remove when Prisma ships a 7.x release bundling mysql2 >=3.22.0 (run `npm audit` to confirm the advisory is gone), or upgrade instead of allowlisting if we ever adopt a MySQL datasource.

allow.reason: MySQL2 decompression-bomb DoS: an unbounded zlib inflate in the compressed MySQL protocol handler. Same provenance as GHSA-3f6p-5ww8-9rcr: mysql2 is bundled by the Prisma CLI (prisma@7.9.1) for MySQL datasources and is never loaded here. This is a PostgreSQL-only app (datasource postgresql, @prisma/adapter-pg / pg) that never opens a MySQL connection, let alone a compressed one, so the vulnerable protocol handler is unreachable at build and runtime.
allow.noFixAvailable: No patched Prisma 7.x release bundles a fixed mysql2 yet; npm's only 'fix' is a Prisma major downgrade. The package never runs in production, so allowlisting with an expiry is preferred over churning the lockfile.
allow.reviewAction: Remove when Prisma ships a 7.x release bundling a patched mysql2 (run `npm audit` to confirm), or if we ever adopt a MySQL datasource.

allow.package: fast-uri (transitive via prisma CLI dev tooling)
allow.reason: fast-uri host confusion via skipped IDN canonicalization on scheme-relative references. fast-uri is a build/dev-time transitive of the Prisma CLI only: prisma@7.9.1 -> @prisma/dev -> @prisma/streams-local -> ajv -> fast-uri. @prisma/dev is Prisma's local development server tooling and is never imported or executed by the production Express app (which talks to Postgres via @prisma/client + @prisma/adapter-pg + pg). fast-uri is never invoked on runtime request data, so the parsing path is unreachable in production.
allow.noFixAvailable: A patched fast-uri (3.1.7) exists but sits deep in the Prisma CLI tree (ajv -> fast-uri); an `overrides` pin did not take (npm kept Prisma's resolved 3.1.5). The real fix is a Prisma CLI upgrade bundling the patched fast-uri; no such 7.x release exists yet. Never runs in production.
allow.reviewAction: Remove when a Prisma 7.x upgrade pulls fast-uri >=3.1.7 (run `npm audit` to confirm the four fast-uri advisories are gone).

allow.package: fast-uri (transitive via prisma CLI dev tooling)
allow.reason: fast-uri SSRF via malformed IPv6 normalization. Reachability identical to GHSA-5jgf-p345-68v8: fast-uri comes only via prisma@7.9.1 -> @prisma/dev -> @prisma/streams-local -> ajv -> fast-uri (Prisma's local dev server tooling), never executed by the production Express app, never invoked on runtime request data. SSRF path unreachable in production.
allow.noFixAvailable: Patched in fast-uri 3.1.7 but pinned deep inside the Prisma CLI tree; no Prisma 7.x release bundles it yet and an overrides pin did not take. Never runs in production.
allow.reviewAction: Remove when a Prisma 7.x upgrade pulls fast-uri >=3.1.7 (run `npm audit` to confirm).
